© Curated Lifestyle on Unsplash+
ADa Wein is a Travel Tomorrow reporter. She is a Belgian-born writer who has lived in Europe, Africa, and the Middle East. She writes about travel, culture, arts, and politics. Ada publishes the newsletter Art & Terror , a weekly press review where politics meets art. She has contributed to Book Salon, Aslan Media, and published children’s stories and fiction, some of which can be found on Ephémérides . Art & Terror was created to explore philosophical debates on political matters through various mediums: essays, analyses, poetry, pictures, and documentaries. ADa lives in Brussels with her two daughters.
A new ranking of the world’s twenty most-visited museums has been published, and China dominates it overwhelmingly. Just over a decade ago, only a handful of Asian museums made the list. Part of the shift comes from a broader definition of what counts as a museum, which now takes in historic palaces and heritage sites.
Compiled by the Themed Entertainment Association (TEA), together with research partner Entertainment + Culture Advisors (ECA) and the Park Database (TPDB), the ranking is based on visitor numbers recorded in 2025.
China dominated the list, with 12 entries, five of which are in its capital, Beijing. It also claims all three spots on the winners’ podium.
The remaining eight spots are shared between France, the United Kingdom and South Korea, with two entries each, while the United States and Vatican City have one each.
The number one spot goes to Beijing’s Palace Museum, better known as the Forbidden City. Once upon a time the residence of Chinese emperors, it now houses a vast collection of imperial treasures, paintings, ceramics, and jade artefacts. It welcomed 19 million people last year.
Second place goes to the Summer Palace, also in Beijing, another remnant of the country’s imperial past. Renowned for its gardens, temples and lakes, it attracted 17,381,000 visitors in 2025.
Beijing’s National Museum of China, tracing the country’s history and civilisation, comes tenth with 6,900,000 visitors, while Prince Kung’s Mansion Museum, a beautifully preserved Qing dynasty residence, ranks fourteen. Beijing’s fifth entry, which also closes the top 20, is the China Science and Technology Museum.
Elsewhere in China, the Emperor Qin Shihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum in Xi’an, home to the famous Terracotta Army, takes third place on the winners’ podium with 10.97 million visitors.
Shenzhen’s Nanshan District Museum, dedicated to local history and cultural heritage, ranks sixth, while another defining chapter of Chinese history is explored at the Opium War Museum in Dongguan (9). The museum retraces the nineteenth-century conflicts between imperial China and Western powers, which marked the beginning of what China has long called its “century of humiliation”.
The Sanxingdui Museum in Guanghan, famous for its extraordinary bronze masks and sculptures, ranks fifteenth, just ahead of Chengdu’s Wuhou Shrine Museum, dedicated to the Three Kingdoms period.
Nanjing Museum, with its massive collection of Chinese art and archaeology, and the Shenyang Palace Museum, a former imperial residence, occupy eighteenth and nineteenth places respectively.
Europe is represented by only five institutions on the list, with Paris and London unsurprisingly leading the way.
Le Louvre in Paris, home to Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa , the Venus de Milo , and countless other masterpieces, comes fourth with just over 9 million visitors in 2025. It remains the most visited museum outside of China.
France’s second entry is the Palace of Versailles (5), famous for its Hall of Mirrors and gardens, with 8.4 million visitors.
London, where many of the major museums offer free admission to their permanent collections, has two entries. The Natural History Museum (7), celebrated for its dinosaur fossils and natural history collections and the British Museum (13), home to the Rosetta Stone and Egyptian antiquities.
The Vatican Museums (8), whose collection includes Michelangelo’s celebrated frescoes in the Sistine Chapel, completes Europe’s representation.
South Korea also has two institutions in the ranking, both in Seoul: Gyeongbokgung Palace (11), the former royal residence of the Joseon dynasty and the National Museum of Korea (12), showcasing Korean art and archaeology.
Across the Atlantic, New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, or the Met, comes seventeenth. Famous for its collections spanning thousands of years and civilisations, it is the only American institution to make the top-20.
Just over a decade ago, London, Paris, and Washington, DC, dominated the list.
In the European top-20, many of the top places are former royal residences, including Versailles, Istanbul’s Topkapı Palace, Vienna’s Schönbrunn Palace and Kraków’s Wawel Royal Castle, alongside archaeological sites such as Pompeii.

Inside White Dwarf 530 – The forces of the Ten Thousand unleashed
Custodes take point in a White Dwarf featuring Ancestor Gods, space pirates and titanic, duelling walkers. Join us as we take a look inside.
Issue 530 kicks off with a lore article exploring Custodian titles and some of the heroic deeds they perform to earn them. Basically, if you ever meet a Custodian, don’t worry about not being able to remember their name!
Once that’s whetted your appetite, you get to see the forces of the Adeptus Custodes in action in a battle report pitting them against an insidious uprising of Genestealer cultists, whose very existence threatens the security of an entire subsector. Or it would if they could shoot straight with their mining lasers.
Worried your kill teams have had it too easy lately? The Tyrant’s Claim introduces a new Joint Ops mission for Kill Team, which finds your forces attempting to hold the line against Huron Blackheart and a cast of his closest ne’er-do-wells. Can you stop them as they venture forth from the Maelstrom to raid your supply lines in the finest piratical tradition?
The White Dwarf team heads over to the Mortal Realms to dig up lots of information about the newest Warhammer Age of Sigmar faction – the Khazalite Holds. There’s background and lore, plus interviews with the team behind the art in the new battletome, and a step-by-step painting guide from the ’Eavy Metal team for the colours of Karak Angaraz.
And what would an issue of White Dwarf be without its namesake? Grombrindal returns with a new Legends warscroll for the main duardin himself, as well as rules for a new Army of Renown – Grombrindal’s Expedition. This army focuses on Old Whitebeard leading a force of like-minded duardin who are able to harness their pioneering spirit into potent tactical advantages.
White Dwarf 530 also features your usual favourites including The Bunker, scenarios of the month for Warhammer 40,000 and Warhammer Age of Sigmar, and handy tearout rules for the Stormsurge and Wraithknight in Titanic Duel.*

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
The train disaster, one of Europe’s deadliest rail incidents this century, killed 69 people, including 54 Spaniards
Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic were among the 69 killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.
Wednesday’s disaster – one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents this century – has seen victims’ relatives endure an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.
A legal body set up to handle the identification work, made up of police and forensics experts, announced in a statement late on Sunday the 10 latest confirmed foreign victims.
It had already announced the deaths of a French and a Portuguese citizen, as well as that of 54 Spaniards.
All but three of the victims are now identified, the statement added.
Three reports for missing people remain active, the authorities said. They concern two Australians and one Japanese citizen.
“As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country,” the statement said.
The accident was Spain’s second high-speed train collision this year and raised fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, after a crash in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people.
The latest disaster struck when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to Spanish company Iryo outside the central village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63km stretch of track, but a control centre authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey while the other train was still.
The tragedy came one month before a 29 November general election in which Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez will seek to overcome unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership.

articles.title_orig: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion deal in AI data-center bet
articles.title_zh: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion deal in AI data-center bet
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology on Monday said it will buy optical components maker Lumentum to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout.
"AI infrastructure is undergoing a fundamental architectural shift toward optical connectivity, creating an opportunity that comes along once in a generation," said Marvell Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy in a release. "The companies that move first and help define this transition will set the standard for decades to come."
Since the tie-up is a fixed ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.
Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.
Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.
Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.
This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.
Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.
Marvell shares slumped 3%, while Lumentum's stock declined about 4% before the bell.

articles.title_orig: Supermarket fridges in Sweden, Ireland overheat amid suspected cyberattacks
articles.title_zh: Supermarket fridges in Sweden, Ireland overheat amid suspected cyberattacks
articles.content_orig:
Suspected cyberattacks have triggered temperatures to rise in grocery store refrigeration systems in a growing number of countries across Europe.
Overnight temperature spikes were recorded in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden. On Monday, retailers and authorities pointed to alleged cyberattacks that underscored the vulnerability of systems that once largely operated mechanically.
The head of ⁠⁠⁠⁠Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, confirmed on Monday to the Reuters news agency that the centre ⁠⁠⁠⁠is responding to ⁠⁠⁠⁠multiple incidents affecting store cooling systems.
“We have in recent weeks … identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” he said.
The temperature of freezers in several Swedish stores rose suddenly overnight, store operators ICA and Coop said, while Swedish retailer Axfood said freezers at a distribution centre for home delivery of groceries in the Gothenburg area were hacked.
SuperValu, Ireland’s third-largest supermarket chain, ⁠⁠⁠⁠said a specific model of refrigeration systems has been affected by a “cyber incident” at 13 of its 223 ⁠⁠⁠⁠stores.
The Belga news agency reported overnight temperature increases at dozens of ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg. They were blamed on a cyberattack, according to the chief ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠executive ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠of refrigeration company,⁠ ⁠⁠⁠Sabcobel.
Stephan Moelans said the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.
Also in Belgium, five Spar shops had their fridge systems attacked, said a spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates the franchise system.
In Estonia, at least one supermarket chain was affected, technology supplier Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR.
“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” Kitman’s CEO Jann Mutso said, without naming the affected chain.
Ahold Delhaize reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month.
The cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets in France raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F), spoiling food and causing fires at several stores.
One Swedish store said in a social media post on Monday that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been set to the same temperature as during the cyberattack in France.
“We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems,” a spokesperson for privately held ICA told Reuters in an email.
Kitman’s Mutso also said that temperatures at the Estonian chain were set to 50 degrees Celsius (122F).
Privately-held retailer Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents.
There has been no claim of responsibility for Monday’s attack, nor the one earlier in France.
However, the incidents help to increase concern regarding hybrid warfare stemming from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran-United States war.
European states have blamed Moscow for a growing number of incidents affecting infrastructure, including via cyberattacks, in recent months. Russia has repeatedly denied involvement in any sabotage or hybrid warfare operations.
“These incidents show that cyberattacks ⁠can disrupt services, affect ⁠businesses and directly affect citizens’ ⁠daily lives”, a ⁠European Commission spokesperson ⁠said, stressing the importance of strengthening ‌cybersecurity across the bloc.
A spokesperson for The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium told Al Jazeera that the rising number of cyberattack incidents, especially those resulting from the targeted use of AI, is an evolving trend.
However, they added, “we may never be able to identify … who is behind this attack”.

articles.title_orig: Goodbye to the toilet brush: the more hygienic alternative more and more bathrooms are switching to
articles.title_zh: Goodbye to the toilet brush: the more hygienic alternative more and more bathrooms are switching to
articles.content_orig:
TheCoolist is a mood board for your headspace.
It sits next to every toilet, usually in a closed holder, and a Finnish cleaning expert says many people keep it far too long. In Scandinavia and Central Europe, home sites report that many households are now swapping the classic bristle toilet brush for a different design. Here’s what is replacing it, why cleaning pros say it’s more hygienic, and what it still can’t do.
According to the Norwegian site Dagens.no , many people are choosing a silicone brush over the traditional plastic one. The reasons it gives: there are no dense bristles for dirt to collect in, so the head rinses clean; the flexible head reaches the edges and hard-to-access areas; it tends to spray less; and it is often sold with a ventilated or wall-mounted holder that lets it dry faster. The site quotes Finnish cleaning expert Mari Breilin, who says plastic brushes should be replaced considerably more often than many people do. The price, it adds, is about the same as many ordinary brushes.
The British testing site Expert Reviews sums it up: bristles are “so tightly packed together that it’s impossible to clean them perfectly,” so “bacteria build-up on the brush is inevitable,” and they “need replacing much more often.” Cleaning expert Isabella Flores, of Sparkly Maid San Diego, told Tom’s Guide that silicone is non-porous, so it doesn’t absorb bacteria and organic matter the way plastic bristles can. It also dries faster and tolerates harsher disinfection, including boiling.
Silicone or not, the routine is what keeps it hygienic. Tom’s Guide recommends:
Silicone is not a miracle. Expert Reviews notes that silicone brushes shaped like regular ones “usually have weak bristles that don’t do a great job on stubborn dirt,” and that flat, spatula-style heads handle grime better, though you have to get used to a different technique. And no brush, silicone or bristle, is built to dissolve the hard mineral ring at the waterline. And whatever you choose, a brush kept damp in a closed holder will still breed bacteria.
For that waterline ring, here’s the best way to remove limescale from the toilet . The bathroom is changing in other ways too, like the option replacing toilet paper , and the floor around the base deserves attention: see why people are spraying vinegar around the toilet .
A flat silicone head, an open holder and a date to replace it. That’s the trick.

U.S. stocks are recovering after Friday's selloff, helped by a slide in oil prices.

articles.title_orig: Karl Bushby completes 28-year, 31,000-mile walk around world and returns to mother’s house
articles.title_zh: Karl Bushby completes 28-year, 31,000-mile walk around world and returns to mother’s house
articles.content_orig:
Former paratrooper Karl Bushby arrives back in Hull and becomes first person to walk continuously across planet
After a 28-year odyssey spanning 29 countries, 36,000 miles, facing down polar bears, kidnappers and a spell in Russian custody, Karl Bushby was finally back in the arms of his long-suffering mother, Angela.
“Where have I been?” he joked as Angela sobbed into his chest with a mix of relief, pride and no doubt the odd sleepless night.
Surrounded by television cameras and with a Sky News helicopter overhead, the 57-year-old was given a hero’s welcome as he completed his record-breaking voyage on foot from Punta Arenas in Chile, the southernmost city on the South American continent, to his home town of Hull on Monday.
“There has never been a welcome home quite like this, I’m sure,” said Bushby, shaking his head in disbelief as he greeted a crowd of well-wishers in the city’s Queen Victoria Square. “This is absolutely madness.”
It has been 28 years since Bushby, then aged 29, left the army to walk the world on what he intended to be a 12-year journey. He finally crossed a misty Humber Bridge back to the city on Sunday – on the same date he set off in 1998.
In that time he has stuck by two simple rules: not to return home until he had fully completed his feat, and not to use transport to advance.
In all, he walked 36,000 miles across four continents, a frozen sea, deserts, jungles and mountains. Quite a trek for a man not keen on walking. “It’s boring as hell,” he told the Guardian last month.
His return on Monday will make Bushby the first person to have walked continuously across the world, visiting 29 countries, having already exceeded the record for the longest unbroken foot journey (far outstripping the 25,000-mile circumference of the world).
The voyage took him across the frozen sea of the Bering strait between Alaska and Russia and across the notorious Darién Gap in Central America. He described last month how he had been threatened at gunpoint, faced down a polar bear, was convicted of being a spy, and been held in custody in Russia and sentenced to deportation.
Bushby strode into Queen Victoria Square like a modern folk hero, his passage only slowed by the dozens of people rushing to shake his hand and take photographs.
Yet for a man who had navigated much of the planet, he did appear to get a little lost on his way through the crowds of his home city. “I’ve no idea which direction I’m going. Everybody point the way,” he said. “Sorry to keep you all waiting – it’s been a while.”
Through the crowd he pushed his heavily loaded trolley, dubbed the Beast 2 (his first one broke down) laden with essentials such as medicine, sleeping bags, headtorches – and two very worn tyres. “Sorry everybody, sorry,” he said as he manoeuvred through the well-wishers.
About three miles away, Angela, 75, was waiting at the gate of Bushby’s childhood home as she had promised. After a tearful embrace, they took a long look at each other.
“You’ve changed a bit,” Bushby told her. “I’m older,” his mother replied through tears. “We both are,” he said. “Well done for hanging in there.”
He was then whisked inside the small terrace house, festooned with union flag bunting, where he was reunited with his son, now 36, and a 12-year-old granddaughter whom he was meeting for the first time.
Earlier on a makeshift stage, Bushby thanked the city for his hero’s welcome. “It took a world to get me here,” he said. “The kindness of strangers – so many, from individuals to nation states, to get me back here. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team: Earth.
“We faced down governments, we faced down some of the hardest challenges, we had to create two world records just to get back here. It was a global effort.”
At one point, the great German film-maker Werner Herzog appeared on stage alongside Bushby, overseeing what will surely be one of the closing scenes in Herzog’s documentary on the 28-year odyssey.
Karl Turner, the Labour MP for Kingston upon Hull East, brought with him a message from the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who congratulated Bushby on his “truly remarkable” feat and thanked him for his service as a paratrooper.
In a statement read on stage by Turner, Burnham said: “Your journey has taken nearly three decades, crossed continents and tested you in ways most of us can barely imagine.
“But today, as you return to the city from which you left 28 years ago, you bring with you something far greater than any world record or a remarkable personal achievement. You bring a story of what can be accomplished through extraordinary determination and self-belief.”
As he was ushered away for a big lunch before the walk to his mother’s house, Bushby had one last message for the city he left in 1998: “I guess I’ll be seeing you around.”

articles.title_orig: Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
articles.title_zh: Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine and Russia have both said air alert apps were hacked on Sunday night after fake messages warning of attacks, including nuclear, were sent to users.
Ukraine's widely used app sent red-level air raid warnings across the country, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv.
A few hours later, Russian authorities said a similar app was hacked after fake alerts, some of which contained foul language, were triggered.
It was unclear who was behind the cyberattacks or whether the two incidents were connected.
Many Ukrainian citizens are used to receiving almost nightly alerts warning of incoming Russian missile and drone attacks. Some told the BBC that, four and a half years into the war, they have disabled the app altogether.
After Sunday night's hack, the country's air force urged people to consult other official channels.
In a post on Telegram, the air force said: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our [Telegram] channel."
The government said it had temporarily disabled the app for maintenance, saying it had "apparently been compromised".
Some of the fake warnings were written in Russian, which would have alerted many users to the fact they were not legitimate.
But Olena, a Kyiv resident, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been alarmed, saying: "The first thought was 'oh my god, I'm not prepared for this'.
"I'm prepared for blackouts, for a cut in central heating and water supply, but not for nuclear attack."
Olena says her husband then received alerts for "street fighting attacks in Kyiv" and another alert, written in Russian.
"After that I understood that somebody had attacked the app, because all notifications we get in Ukrainian."
In Russia, the government said one of its air raid alert apps had also been targeted by "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public".
A purported screenshot of a fake alert was shared on Telegram by Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory.
It warned some users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".
The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of [things] getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".
On Monday morning there was no sense the messages had caused widespread panic in Russia and the incident did not feature prominently on media outlets.
Asked about the breach, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not address it specifically but said all Russian government internet resources were "one way or another... under constant cyberattacks", including the presidential site, which is targeted "round the clock".
He said the proliferation of AI technology was contributing to an increase in cyberattacks.
Russia's emergencies ministry said on Monday that the app's "full functionality will be restored by the end of the day" and the hack had not impacted the wider alert system.
While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Those responsible for the hack on Russia's system have likely had the capability to launch such an attack for some time but decided to hold off until Ukraine's alert app was compromised, cyber experts told the BBC.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament, said the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko told the BBC that Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts", adding "this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions".
He continued: "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities."
Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think it's the first time [a hack of this kind] happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last."
The alerts in Ukraine were sent minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's frontline Kherson region, which was implemented last Tuesday. It had been brokered in part by US First Lady Melania Trump to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Fighting continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place. In the city of Dnipro alone, 15 people were killed in an attack on a train platform on Thursday.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Tech stocks aren't getting shredded for any old reason. It's actually very fundamental: Free cash flow is drying up for Big Tech leaders, and capex is rising dramatically.
Investors are questioning whether this ratio is totally out of whack, given more realistic growth projections for AI.
The combined capex of Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft rose by $36.9 billion in the third quarter to $201.9 billion, the team at The Kobeissi Letter calculated (chart below). This figure has more than doubled over the past 12 months, and is up a staggering 356% since the first quarter of 2024.
Big Tech has now spent $1.6 trillion on capex over the last three years, the strategists say. At the same time, the combined free cash flow of these companies fell $33.1 billion last quarter to a negative $26.4 billion, its lowest on record. Free cash flow among these tech beasts has fallen by $88.2 billion over the last year. Only Microsoft reported positive free cash flow in the third quarter. Looking ahead, the strategists estimate these four companies plan to spend another $232 billion on capex in the fourth quarter.
The AI trade saw a serious slamming on Friday, with more than $1 trillion in market value wiped away as investors fretted about the weakening cash flow profiles of Big Tech.
"The AI narrative is cracking as profitability concerns intensify," warned Miller Tabak chief markets strategist Matt Maley.

articles.title_orig: Record reward offered for capture of fugitive cocaine kingpin dubbed "Chubby Jos"
articles.title_zh: Record reward offered for capture of fugitive cocaine kingpin dubbed "Chubby Jos"
articles.content_orig:
Dutch authorities are offering a record reward of 2 million euros ($2.2 million) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers , one of Europe's most-wanted drug traffickers, currently hiding in Sierra Leone.
The arrest of Leijdekkers, also known as "Bolle Jos" ("Chubby Jos"), is "the highest priority for the Public Prosecution Service and the police," said Dutch prosecutors in a statement, multiplying by 10 their previous reward.
Leijdekkers is considered to be one of the key players in the international cocaine trade.
A court in Rotterdam sentenced him in absentia in 2024 to 24 years in prison for drug shipments totaling nearly 7,000 kilos of cocaine, an armed robbery, and ordering a "liquidation."
He has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
Dutch police have tracked the 35-year-old to Sierra Leone.
Any information shared with prosecutors will be kept secret, the Dutch authorities said in a statement.
In January 2025, Dutch authorities said they were "absolutely certain" he was hiding out in Sierra Leone. The BBC reported that Dutch prosecutor Wim de Bruin said the fugitive's return to the Netherlands was of "the highest priority."
Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of officials as high as President Julius Maada Bio have sparked speculation that the cocaine baron has cozied up to Sierra Leone's political class — including the president's daughter.
Suspicions that he was in Sierra Leone arose after the country's first lady, Fatima Bio, posted pictures and a video on social media that showed a man strongly resembling Leijdekkers at a religious service, also attended by President Bio.
Leijdekkers is also believed to be involved in the disappearance and death of Naima Jillal, a woman who went missing in 2019 after she got into a car in Amsterdam, according to Europol . Intercepted messages allegedly showed that Leijdekkers "played an important role in Jillal's disappearance," the agency said.
"For a long time, there was no trace of Naima Jillal, until photos of a woman believed to be her were found on a phone seized in the Marengo investigation," Europol said. "The photos show that she was most likely tortured and is probably no longer alive."

articles.title_orig: Dell XPS Googlebook Review: Beautiful Hardware For A Useless Platform
articles.title_zh: Dell XPS Googlebook Review: Beautiful Hardware For A Useless Platform
articles.content_orig:
Googlebook OS still needs a ton of work.
I can think of a few reasons to buy a Googlebook , but they're all pretty dystopian. Maybe every other computing platform has succumbed to a super AI-powered virus, leaving a Googlebook as your only option. Or perhaps Google has taken over the world and has started hunting down people who use Windows, Linux or macOS. In a world where a Googlebook is your only option, then the $1,000 Dell XPS Googlebook is probably the one to get. But in the real world, where you can get the exact same XPS hardware running on more flexible platforms with better developer support, the XPS Googlebook seems practically pointless.
But let's back up a bit and talk about Googlebook OS, Google's new laptop platform that's a combination of both Android and ChromeOS. It supports Android apps natively, it can synchronize and mirror apps from your Android phone, and it has Google's Gemini AI integrated throughout its interface. Technically, Googlebook OS should be an upgrade from ChromeOS, a platform built entirely around Google's web browser. But, after testing this laptop for the last week, I'd go so far as to say the entire Googlebook concept is a failure.
Who really wants a laptop running unoptimized Android apps? Why buy into an untested Google platform just to synchronize your Android phone, especially when you can mirror and sync Android device texts on Windows and Linux? And why would you pay the same exact price as a Windows PC for a computer that does so much less? While Apple, Microsoft and PC makers are sweating to push the computing industry forward this year, most notably with the launch of NVIDIA's RTX Spark and Apple's redesigned touchscreen MacBook Pro , Google has given us a new platform that is in many ways less useful than its aging Chromebooks.
For its first (and I'm hoping only) Googlebook, Dell took its recent XPS 13 design and refashioned it for Google's new OS. It still has a slim 2.2-pound metal case, making it one of the lightest systems in this size range, and it sports a 13.4-inch InfinityEdge screen. It's powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite chip with 16GB of RAM — the same hardware on the $1,000 Windows 11 XPS 13. There are only two USB-C ports on either side of the XPS 13 Googlebook, and, unfortunately, there's no headphone jack.
A multi-colored "Glowbar" occasionally lights up on the rear of the XPS 13 — something that Google highlights as one of the defining features of Googlebook OS — but it's ultimately superfluous. It can show your charging status and battery level, but it's not exactly solving any major problems for laptop users.
It's not unusual to see PC makers reusing their designs — many companies are also recycling their existing work for NVIDIA's RTX Spark chip. But at least that platform has a few halo products designed specifically for it, like the Surface Laptop Ultra. There's nothing highlighting what's truly special about Googlebook OS — arguably because there's not exactly much to show off.
I could tell you that the XPS Googlebook has a very nice screen, a comfortable keyboard and a very accurate touchpad. I could tell you that its slim design and light weight makes it easy to tote around without weighing down your bag. But really, you could have learned all of that from my review of the standard XPS 13 with Windows 11. Everything good about this system comes from Dell's excellent design work.
Once I started using Googlebook OS, though, it became instantly clear that Googlebook OS is simply a hot mess. It's fine for web browsing with Chrome and accessing Google apps like Gmail and Calendar, but support for Android apps via the Google Play store is mostly disappointing. Slack only works as a mobile Android app, allowing you to see a single channel or direct message, but there's no wider desktop view like you'd see on Windows or macOS. You also can't easily react to messages and images in Slack — instead, you have to perform a long click, as you would on a normal Android phone. Evernote, meanwhile, doesn't appear at all on the Googlebook Play Store. (And yes, I still use Evernote a ton. There are dozens of us!)
"Desktop optimized" Android apps function more like you'd expect on other laptop platforms. Notability, CapCut Pad and Luminar all offer more fully-featured apps for taking AI notes and editing media, but they're only useful if those apps are already part of your workflow. I can't imagine too many people will change their editing process just to find something compatible with Googlebook OS.
Using the XPS Googlebook for my typical workflow often felt like pulling teeth. While Chrome worked fine for web browsing, resizing a photo required an odyssey through several different apps until I stumbled into Pixlr, a desktop-optimized editing app that only lets you resize an image when exporting it. Adobe Lightroom only seemed to let me resize a picture by cropping it (and it also kept bugging me to subscribe to Lightroom Premium to unlock more editing features). I eventually discovered that the standalone Viewer app has an easy way to resize images, something that isn't present in the default Photos app.
With no support for Audacity, I had to use Lexis Audio Editor to make some tweaks to a podcast file, but its basic interface seemed unsuited to more complicated edits. I might as well have just used an online editor like Audiomass (which, by the way, works just fine on Chromebooks). I also had to rely on Evernote's website to write this review, which required logging in every single time I turned on the XPS Googlebook, because the Evernote Android app was unavailable. I also eventually gave up on the Slack Android app and started using its web interface, which at least let me see all of my channels and direct messages.
I'm used to computers being gateways to sophisticated software and healthy developer support. Using the XPS Googlebook felt like being trapped in a computing stripmall: It's hobbled together by a variety of small apps of varying quality. Thank goodness for web apps, at least.
It's worth noting that Chromebooks also supported Android apps, so I don't believe there was actually a huge demand for a new Android-based computing platform.
I also wasn't impressed by any of the other Googlebook features: Syncing your Android phone to a Googlebook sounds nice in theory, but in reality it leads to redundant notifications if you have the same apps installed on both systems. You can also mirror an Android app from your phone — but again, why would you do that when you can run the app directly on the Googlebook? Given that you can already mirror Android phones and synchronize texts on Windows computers, I'm not sure why anyone would jump into a whole new platform just for these features.
Google being Google, of course, the company also crammed in as many Gemini AI features as it could into this platform. You can ask questions or edit media on the Gemini app, or wiggle the mouse pointer to ask the AI about things you encounter on the web or inside of apps. Gemini did a decent job of answering questions about products that we've featured on Engadget, but unless you absolutely want to lean on Google's AI, there really is no reason to buy a whole laptop just to have Gemini baked into everything.
Google's Rambler AI dictation feature, which lets you dictate text by speaking naturally, is also built into Googlebook OS, and from my testing it seemed to work pretty well. But it doesn't show you the text as you're speaking — it just shows a moving purple waveform, and that sometimes makes it hard to gather your thoughts or see what you were previously thinking. This is a big downside compared to just typing or using old-school dictation that used to be available on Android, but at least Rambler did a good job of cutting out natural "ums" and "uhhs," and it also formatted the text pretty well.

articles.title_orig: China polysilicon prices hold amid market standoff, spot-futures gap
articles.title_zh: China polysilicon prices hold amid market standoff, spot-futures gap
articles.content_orig:
The China Mono Premium, the OPIS assessment for mono-grade polysilicon used in n-type ingot production, was unchanged at CNY 38.786 ($5.82)/kg, or CNY 0.081/W, according to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Oct. 27.
According to market participants, the fundamentals of the Chinese polysilicon market remain unchanged, with the market continuing to be characterized by manufacturers holding firm to full-cost-based offers while downstream buyers show limited willingness to accept current prices. This has kept prices largely at a standstill, with inventory levels exceeding 500,000 metric tons (MT) further prolonging the impasse.
Industry participants widely noted that futures prices, which remain significantly below mainstream spot prices, have provided a degree of balance to the ongoing standoff between upstream suppliers and downstream buyers. According to data from the Guangzhou Futures Exchange on Oct. 26, settlement prices for polysilicon futures contracts for delivery between November 2026 and October 2027 ranged from a low of CNY 33.620/kg to a high of CNY 37.180/kg, with even the highest about 4.14% below the latest spot assessment.
Market participants explained that actual spot transactions continue to be concluded at higher prices than futures contracts, partly because customers with long-term purchase agreements still need to procure some material in the spot market. To offset the higher procurement costs, these buyers also source relatively lower-priced polysilicon from futures traders, helping to balance their overall purchasing costs.
One trade participant said that futures traders had been gradually selling off previously accumulated stocks of low-priced polysilicon into the spot market. However, the availability of this lower-priced material is expected to diminish over time. The participant added that manufacturers adhering to the industry self-discipline agreement appear determined not to sell polysilicon at prices below CNY 40/kg during the fourth quarter. As low-priced supplies dwindle and manufacturers maintain their price stance, futures prices are expected to gradually rise, allowing actual spot transaction prices to find a new balance between futures prices and prevailing spot offers.
Separately, an industry source said the China Photovoltaic Industry Association would organize monitoring activities to oversee the implementation of polysilicon production cuts planned for the fourth quarter, adding that this gives the market a degree of confidence and expectation that prices will remain stable. However, no official confirmation or disclosure regarding these activities was available at the time of reporting.
Looking ahead, an upstream participant expected mainstream polysilicon offers to remain unchanged until the Lunar New Year in early February 2027. Meanwhile, prices offered by manufacturers that have not signed the pricing self-discipline agreement, along with polysilicon futures prices, are expected to remain below mainstream spot offers.
The Global Polysilicon Marker (GPM), the benchmark for polysilicon produced outside China, was assessed at $19.234/kg, or $0.040/W, unchanged from the previous week.
Both manufacturers and buyers in the global polysilicon market continued to face mounting pressure. One trade participant noted that some suppliers had reduced their China-based polysilicon sales teams to just a handful of people, underscoring the increasingly weak demand environment.
On the demand side, a source at an integrated manufacturer said that certain long-term contract holders with cell manufacturing facilities in the U.S. could still absorb around 300 MT of global polysilicon per month. While this volume provides some support for demand, the contribution remains relatively small and limited in scope.
Certain long-term contract holders, despite being in poor financial condition, reportedly continue to purchase global polysilicon at a loss due to their contractual obligations. However, the pricing mechanisms embedded in long-term contracts negotiated several years ago have given buyers some room to negotiate, potentially allowing these agreements to remain in effect despite challenging market conditions.
In the near term, industry participants generally expect the main sources of global polysilicon supply to remain U.S.-produced material and lower-priced polysilicon from other origins. In addition, the framework established under the Section 232 outcome has enabled limited volumes of compliant Chinese polysilicon to continue flowing into Southeast Asia.

articles.title_orig: Iran has a 2-day plan to reopen Strait, resume nuclear talks with US, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Iran has a 2-day plan to reopen Strait, resume nuclear talks with US, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Iran said Monday it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the United States if Washington meets its demands, shortening a process originally expected to take seven days.
The announcement came as the region braces for possible renewed fighting, even as Iran’s top diplomat said Sunday that he hoped the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.”
Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the U.S. met seven conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Iran now says ships passing through the reopened strait would have to follow a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman and travel under Iranian supervision. Separately, Iranian officials have said the U.S. must lift sanctions on Iranian oil sales and agree to a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said the plan remained the basis for negotiations with Washington through mediators, despite the shorter implementation timeline. “This once again demonstrates Iran’s good-faith approach,” he added.
Baghaei gave no indication that Tehran had changed its demands or that Washington had accepted its proposal.
President Donald Trump has alternated between pursuing diplomacy and threatening heavy bombing of Iran in his public comments.

articles.title_orig: PlayStation Is Engaging in a “Firmware War” Against Jailbreakers, as Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI Minimum Firmware Requirement Has Reportedly Changed
articles.title_zh: PlayStation Is Engaging in a “Firmware War” Against Jailbreakers, as Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI Minimum Firmware Requirement Has Reportedly Changed
articles.content_orig:
Over the past few weeks, the hacking scene for current-generation gaming systems has made significant strides thanks to the advancement of AI models. While console jailbreaking is normally a significant issue that console manufacturers try to resolve as quickly as possible, Sony has an additional reason to act as quickly as possible, as it cannot afford to leave any hole unpatched on PlayStation 5 due to the release of Rockstar Games ' Grand Theft Auto VI .
A month after the 14.10.00 PlayStation 5 system software update, the 14.22.00.00 update has gone live today. This minor update introduces some “security fixes to the system software,” so there's little doubt that this update is the new move in the firmware war Sony engaged with jailbreakers.
What makes the release of this new PlayStation 5 system software update more interesting is how it is reportedly strictly related to Grand Theft Auto VI 's launch on November 19 . According to PlayStation Game Size , which tracks updates on the PlayStation Network database, the next entry in the Rockstar Games ' series will now require firmware 14.22.00 instead of 14.10.00 , which is unprecedented.
However, extreme situations call for extreme measures. With Grand Theft Auto VI set to sell the most on PlayStation 5 , Sony cannot allow any opening to piracy, as in the age of AI , even the smallest software vulnerability could have big consequences. And piracy could be only one of the consequences, as the game could be emulated and even recompiled into a native PC port before its official release , which would be disastrous for both Sony and Rockstar Games .
As jailbreakers and hackers will hardly stand down just because Sony is releasing multiple PlayStation 5 firmware updates in rapid succession, I expect this confrontation to continue even past November 19 , when Grand Theft Auto VI releases. Hopefully, things are not taken to an extreme that would lead to real consequences for paying customers.

articles.title_zh: European supermarkets hit by new fridge cyber attack
articles.content_orig:
Chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg say fridge temperatures rose overnight, similar to hack of French stores
Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have said the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers in dozens of stores rose overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of food losses in France.
Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet on Monday that six of ​its stores ‌had been ​affected, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.
The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​cybersecurity ‌incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said an “IT incident” ​had hit fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg.
A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the supermarket chain had established that temperatures in the cooling systems had increased, adding that the incident was being investigated.
Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets were affected, including five Spar outlets, multiple Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations, and a number of smaller Proxy Delhaize minimarkets.
“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which specialises in refrigeration system installations, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid.”
French ⁠police said in October that hackers had seized control of cooling units at ⁠up to 700 supermarkets in a large-scale attack that led to heavy losses of chilled and frozen foods and underlined the vulnerability of internet-connected systems.
Hackers had remotely overridden the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C. The Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains were among those affected.
Stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products, with many suffering losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). Two stores in Alsace reported a combined loss of €270,000.
Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss.

They disabled alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours. Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.
The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigatiion into the French attack, saying damage included “food losses and fires”, and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, to investigate.
ANSSI subsequently confirmed that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted in the attack.

articles.title_orig: This $48 e-paper display can be whatever you want it to be
articles.title_zh: This $48 e-paper display can be whatever you want it to be
articles.content_orig:
One of the most useful gadgets in my kitchen is now a screen that never asks me for anything.
I recently bought a $48 DIY display kit from Seeed Studio (yes, that’s three E’s), developed in collaboration with TRMNL , that lets me display whatever I want, using whichever software ecosystem I prefer.
I previously built something similar by modding a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, which was selling for around $30 on eBay during a liquidation. The Lenovo device was only ever intended for business-to-business video, but it does a decent job of running a fork of LineageOS . Unfortunately, its limited RAM makes it sluggish. So when I came across the TRMNL kit and its e-paper display, I was sold.
I’d have an always-on display that shows me the information I want, with no subscription required. And since the screen populates automatically, I would never have to wrestle with a slow interface.
The Seeed Studio kit and TRMNL ecosystem aren’t trying to compete with products like the recently announced Apple HomeView , a $299 home hub designed to get the whole family interacting with it. If anything, the TRMNL kit is the HomeView’s antithesis. It’s designed to be entirely passive: The e-paper display stays on, cycling through potentially useful information on your desk or in your kitchen, from calendars and weather to news and all sorts of ideas thought up by its community members.
TRMNL, the platform company, was founded by indie hardware enthusiast Ryan Kulp in 2023 . Its first e-paper device launched via crowdfunding in 2024.
Seeed Studio provides the hardware. The established Shenzhen open hardware company is best known for its XIAO microcontroller boards.
In March 2025, Seeed teased an XIAO e-paper panel on social media, prompting a community member to ask whether it could run TRMNL firmware. The question brought the two teams together, and in July 2025, they announced an official partnership to develop a DIY e-paper kit combining Seeed’s hardware designs with TRMNL’s firmware packages.
Seeed designs and manufactures the hardware, while TRMNL maintains the firmware, plugins, and hosted service. But you’ll still need to make some decisions about how to set up the kit. There are three ways to get it running, depending on your budget and how comfortable you are with managing software yourself.
The stock TRMNL setup connects you with the company’s “ BYOD ecosystem ” (bring your own device), letting you use trmnl.com as your information server with a 14-day free trial. After that, you’ll need to pay a one-time $50 license fee to keep your device connected to TRMNL servers.
If you’d rather go your own way, Seeed offers software options, including Home Assistant compatibility, that don’t require a TRMNL connection or license. You can also access the SenseCraft Seeedash platform, which includes a plugin repository and design workspace. It’s worth checking out the options before committing to a $50 TRMNL license. The browser-based platform also includes a firmware-flashing tool Seeed describes as simple enough for anyone to use.
If you already have a server up and running, you can point the device right at it. Terminus is TRMNL’s open source container for this setup. The Terminus GitHub page describes the BYOS as providing “privacy first functionality by empowering you to run your own private server, network, and devices. You own the stack and the data.”
The e-paper display and control board simply ping an API to retrieve the information to display. You can even write plugins in HTML, which the screen renders as a bitmap. The trade-off is that your server needs to stay online, and maintaining it may bring some system-admin headaches some users may want to avoid. But hey, that’s why there are options.
Two official case designs are available for 3D printing: a triangular prism and an L-shaped case. I went for the latter, and although I’d hoped assembly would be as simple as plugging everything in and slotting the pieces into place, it proved to be a bit more involved.
The kit came with all the hardware I needed, with one slight hiccup: I’d forgotten to order a case or display stand. Fortunately, TRMNL is a proper DIY project, and there are print files available for recommended stand setups. A quick print at my local library’s Bambu printer and $8 solved the problem. I probably should have chosen something other than “dealer’s choice” for the PLA color, as I ended up with a bright canary yellow device case. At least it stands out on my kitchen countertop.
I’d recommend trying the prism shell design over the L-style case I chose because the latter required me to cut a channel for the ribbon cable extension. It wasn’t a huge deal for a project like this, but you may need to do some extra work and fiddle with the fit. You’ll also need needle-nose pliers to remove the print’s support trees from the narrow space.
Before trying to fit everything into the printed case, I wanted to make sure the hardware worked, so I connected the parts on my workbench. The case-less assembly couldn’t be simpler: Connect the battery or a USB-C power source, plug the display directly into the board, and you’re good to go. From there, connect your phone or tablet to the device’s Wi-Fi and enter your local Wi-Fi credentials.
If you attempt this build, be aware that it involves some delicate parts. The FPC is extremely fragile and can break if you force it to bend in a direction it doesn’t want to go (say, around the sharp angle of an L-shaped case). Getting the cable to conform to the design was challenging; I tried using tweezers to coax the cable around the bend but got nowhere fast.
Connecting and routing the ribbon cable extension was the most stressful part of the assembly. The case design just doesn’t accommodate the path the ribbon cable naturally wants to take. Following a helpful tip from a commenter on MakerWorld, I managed to snake the cable through the narrow passage by attaching a bit of paper tape to the end of the ribbon connector.
After powering on the kit for the first time, you’ll see the TRMNL logo and a QR code on the e-paper display. Scanning the code redirects you to a “ How to set up a new device ” guide written by Kulp, the TRMNL creator. The guide had been updated just 15 minutes before I clicked the link—a promising sign of a living document that is constantly evolving.
I wasn’t planning to use the trmnl.com service, but I wanted to get a sense of what it offered for its $50 access fee. The 14-day “free” trial is a misnomer, though. Before you can register your device, you’ll need to enter your credit card information and pay $1 for access. After plopping down a buck, the next screen welcomed me to my trial.
After registering your kit’s MAC address with trmnl.com, you’ll receive what the service calls a “friendly code,” a much shorter identifier that’s easier to remember than an entire MAC address. From there, you can install plugins to display content on a schedule throughout the day.
The options are vast. The marketplace contains standard fare like Google Calendar, weather, and stock quotes, alongside more niche offerings like rotating factoids about the Ferengi Rules of Acquisition in Star Trek .
If you’re looking for a hassle-free solution that “just works,” it’s hard to fault the package trmnl.com has put together. I’m a fan of any service that offers a one-time license fee over yet another forever subscription, and I think $50 is a fair price for the people behind the platform to be compensated for their work. After all, it handles all the rendering; the device simply displays information pulled from the APIs.
On the Seeed side, there’s SenseCraft, a similar marketplace to trmnl.com’s but without the license fee. The website offers a browser-based flashing tool that promises to “flash official firmware from the browser. No coding. No terminal. Just clicks.”

US stocks climbed on Monday as investors regained risk appetite ahead of another packed week of earnings, midterm elections, and a key jobs report.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.8%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) added 0.5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) jumped 0.6%, attempting a comeback after a tech rout dragged stocks last week.
Markets were poised to bounce back after an AI-fueled sell-off that saw the Nasdaq Composite lose 5.2% during the month of October. Chipmakers and other tech names rebounded ahead of the market open, though Apple ( AAPL ) shares dipped slightly in the lead-up to the iPhone maker's earnings report after the bell on Monday. Investors also got a second look at an amended version of Anthropic's S-1 filing.
Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) rose slightly to trade near $78,000 per token after cryptocurrencies took a hit following a $6.3 billion hack of Binance , which investigators are calling the biggest crypto hack in history .
Crude oil prices, meanwhile, dropped amid reports that the US and Iran are seeking a diplomatic resolution to the war in the Middle East. Brent crude futures ( BZ=F ), the international benchmark, traded near $106 per barrel.
On the economic data front, investors will get a reading on US manufacturing activity and prices paid. The calendar for the rest of the week will feature several pieces of labor market data, culminating in the government's October jobs report on Friday.
US stocks opened higher Monday as investors begin November with another week packed with earnings , crucial labor market data and the midterm elections.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.7%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) added 0.5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) jumped 0.7%.
Investors also got a fresh look at Anthropic. The artificial intelligence company filed an amended version of its S-1 filing shortly before Monday's open. Later Monday, investors will also get a reading on US manufacturing activity and prices paid in October.
Binance has seen $3.64 billion in outflows since it gradually restored user withdrawals following the largest crypto hack in history, which the FBI linked to North Korea.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said that it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and approximately $1.01 billion in deposits. Binance detailed that the resulting net outflows represent just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets under management.
Binance was hit late Thursday by a hack that investigators said impacted roughly $6.3 billion in funds, with roughly half of those assets frozen.
On Monday, the exchange said it has covered approximately 95% of the impacted amount. The outstanding 5% consists of smaller tokens outside of the top 10 cryptocurrencies, whose assets are less liquid and will take longer to source.
In pursuit of plans to enter the US wireless market, Elon Musk-led SpaceX ( SPCX ) is reportedly exploring a potential acquisition of Boost Mobile or access to its network.
Verizon ( VZ ), AT&T ( T ) and T-Mobile ( TMUS ) have reportedly rejected SpaceX's requests to use their wireless networks, according to a report from the Washington Post.
SpaceX has since held discussions with EchoStar ( ECHO ), Boost Mobile's parent company, about a potential partnership or acquisition, the report said. Shares of EchoStar are up roughly 5% in premarket trading.
A deal could give SpaceX access to Boost Mobile's network agreements, providing an entry point into the estimated $235 billion US wireless market.
The move would expand Musk's business empire beyond rockets and Starlink, opening another potential revenue stream for SpaceX.
When AI stocks get hit, investors have found a place to hide. It's the company that has mostly sat out the AI spending race — Apple ( AAPL ).
Chip stocks have had plenty of rough days this year, and Apple has mostly shrugged them off. On the 46 days the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) fell 2% or more, Apple rose on 30, about two out of every three.
That's new. From 1994 through last year, Apple rose on only about 1 in 6 of those days, and no year came anywhere close to this one, by Yahoo Finance's calculations.
Apple and chip stocks have basically stopped moving together. Apple's correlation with the chip index — a measure of how closely two assets move in step — turned negative in July and hit its lowest level on record in September.
Apple ( AAPL ) will report its fourth quarter earnings after the bell Monday, providing investors with a glimpse of early iPhone 18 Pro sales. Yahoo Finance's Dan Howley previews what to expect:
The iPhone Duo went up for preorder on Oct. 16 and went on sale Oct. 23, missing Apple's fiscal Q4, though the company could still offer color on demand.
This will also be Apple's first earnings call with new CEO John Ternus , who took over the role from Tim Cook on Sept. 1.
For the quarter, Apple is expected to report earnings per share (EPS) of $2 on revenue of $113.46 billion, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus estimates. The company saw EPS of $1.85 and revenue of $102.46 billion in the same period last year.
Yahoo Finance's Ben Werschkul reports:
The 2026 campaign has featured bipartisan calls for action on pharmaceuticals, the housing market, and AI data centers, a sign that this trio of sectors may be in focus in Washington no matter which party prevails on Tuesday.
The critical comments are especially notable coming from Republicans as the campaign enters its final days. Democratic rhetoric about reining in big business is nothing new, but the GOP's focus indicates both an increased willingness within the party to adopt a populist stance and a potential openness to strike deals next year in the new power-sharing landscape.
And the high likelihood that Democrats will win control of at least one chamber of Congress could elevate these issues — with or without President Trump's support.
The coming year is likely to feature "meaningful opportunities and risks for key sectors," Stifel chief Washington policy strategist Brian Gardner wrote in a recent note to clients.
With another Big Tech company reporting earnings today (Apple ( AAPL )) after the Street gave punishing post-earnings reactions to Alphabet ( GOOG ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) stocks last week, Yahoo Finance's Jake Conley offers some perspective on the market mood:
It was a deeply red week for the tech sector after a slew of earnings failed to give investors the signs of strength they were looking (and hoping) for.
At Alphabet, a miss on both revenue and profit sent shares falling 13% as Sundar Pichai said that while the company's search division had grown, the money wasn't keeping up as AI cuts into search monetization.
Down the street at Amazon, a double miss on both earnings and revenue triggered a sell-off that couldn't be stopped by strong cloud growth in AWS.
And we can't forget Intel, where a beat on earnings and in-line revenue were overshadowed by weakness in PC sales, attributed to heightened memory costs. That company lost a quarter of its value after the report, falling over 28%.
But there's a conundrum for investors in these earnings reports. As Barron's associate editor Al Root said to Yahoo Finance, the numbers weren't all bad; it's more like investors have gotten more demanding.
"It's not that the earnings were awful, it's just that it wasn't enough to support the market," Root said on "The 8:30." He added, "The level of nerves going into earnings season was so high, like everybody was waiting for the shoe to drop."

articles.title_orig: Supermarket freezers in Belgium, Sweden and Luxembourg hit by suspected cyber-attack
articles.title_zh: Supermarket freezers in Belgium, Sweden and Luxembourg hit by suspected cyber-attack
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away, according to local media reports.
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
It is unclear who is behind the apparent attack.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

The Pokémon Company is no stranger to a little over-hyping every now and then, but its latest bit of marketing has us seriously thinking that there is a big announcement in the pipeline.
You see, TPC is counting down to... something. As brought to our attention by Serebii 's Joe Merrick , the company has been sharing images on social media of its 30th anniversary icons , with a number underneath. Interestingly, these numbers decrease by the number of hours that have passed between each post — 1,025 on 18th October, 843 on 26th, 676 today.
Keeping the countdown going, this means that we'll hit zero on 30th November at 2pm UTC (thanks for doing the maths there, Joe!). The latest post even came with a full message under the logo, roughly translating to "Continue with Pokémon".
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 854k
Hmm . The big question is, what's this all about? 2pm UTC sure feels like the right time for a big announcement (it's when most eyes, worldwide, will be on it), and we can't imagine that TPC would put this much planning into something inconsequential.
What is it, then? Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire were rumoured to be coming to NSO last month, could it be that? Is it time we got another look at Winds and Waves , perhaps with a fire release date attached? Is there another full Pokémon Presents around the corner? Only time will tell, but it sure is an exciting prospect.
We'll be keeping an eye on the countdown throughout November and will let you know when any major news comes out of it.

James Titcomb is The Telegraph's Technology Editor and has covered the tech industry for a decade from Silicon Valley and London. He can be reached at james.titcomb@telegraph.co.uk and on X at @jamestitcomb
Tech companies including Elon Musk’s SpaceX and the ChatGPT owner OpenAI are rationing use of their AI systems over soaring running costs.
Mr Musk said revenues from Grok Bot, an AI agent developed by SpaceX’s xAI, were not sufficient to meet the “unsustainably high” costs of operating the system.
It came as OpenAI also introduced restrictions on some users amid a stock market panic over the growing costs of AI and hundreds of billions of dollars in associated debt.
Investors have raised concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom owing to the high costs of running the systems, widespread competition and uncertainty about customers’ willingness to pay.
Users pay up to $200 (£149) a month for Grok, xAI’s competitor to ChatGPT and Claude. Grok Bot, a feature of the service, can navigate websites, respond to emails and log into accounts on users’ behalf, allowing them to offload work to the bot.
However, several users found over the weekend that their monthly usage limits had been cut in half. “It was 33pc and suddenly it became 66pc,” one wrote. Others found they had surpassed usage limits overnight.
Mr Musk wrote on X: “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.” He later responded to one user suggesting they upgrade to a more expensive plan.
OpenAI said that next month it would merge the monthly allowances of two ChatGPT features, Codex and Chat.
The limits had previously been separate, so combining them means users of both could hit usage caps more quickly. While the company said higher-paying users would get greater allowances in response, it did not make the same promises for those on cheaper subscriptions.
Anthropic has also limited some users’ allowances in recent days.
High-powered AI systems are notoriously expensive to run because of the electricity, chips and data centre capacity needed to process instructions. Costs are higher in so-called agentic systems, which can carry out tasks, than in simple chatbots such as ChatGPT.
Anthropic has said they cost between four and 15 times more to operate than chats. Agents such as Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots have become increasingly popular in recent weeks.
Mr Musk’s comments come amid rising concerns about the cost of AI.
Google’s parent company, Alphabet, suffered a record-breaking $500bn market-value loss last week, in part because it raised AI spending forecasts. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index suffered its worst month for more than a year, wiping around $2tn off the world’s biggest tech companies.
Rising interest rates have led to a panic about the substantial sums of debt taken on by data centre developers and other AI companies.
Mr Musk said last week that SpaceX had raised $40bn in debt to purchase Nvidia chips.
