articles.title_zh: Defense, healthcare, crypto and AI: How the midterm election could affect stocks
articles.content_orig:
Lockheed Martin gets about 70% of its sales from the U.S. government. Medicaid accounts for three-quarters of Molina Healthcare's premium revenue . Coinbase is waiting on Congress to finish writing the rules for cryptocurrency .
For some of the biggest U.S. companies, Washington is part of the business model. Now, the midterm election could change who holds the leverage.
A Democratic victory in either or both chambers of Congress would grant the party new leverage to investigate companies , challenge federal spending and demand legislative concessions. But their reach would have limits: President Donald Trump would retain his veto and broad authority over tariffs, immigration and federal regulation.
Historically, stocks have performed well under divided government. Under Republican presidents, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 23% in the year after midterms when Congress was split, compared with 16% when Democrats controlled both chambers, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis published Thursday. Analysts often attribute the pattern in part to congressional gridlock limiting sweeping policy changes.
Still, some analysts caution against assuming that pattern will repeat.
"We don't think that blueprint holds up this time around, and we still see plenty of reasons to be constructive on the U.S. equity market," said Ariana Salvatore , head of U.S. public policy research at Morgan Stanley.
For investors, the midterm election could reshape which businesses preserve their advantages in Washington, particularly in industries such as defense , healthcare , banking and artificial intelligence .
"There are some policy changes that might be market moving, at least for certain segments," said Jeff Buchbinder , chief equity strategist at LPL Financial.
Control of either the House or Senate would give Democrats committee gavels and subpoena power, allowing them to demand documents, compel testimony and haul executives before public hearings.
Companies are already getting a preview.
On Oct. 21, Sen. Richard Blumenthal , D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sought records tied to Trump's White House ballroom from donors including Cisco , Salesforce , ServiceNow and Kraken . Apple and Nvidia each committed $25 million to the project, according to records obtained by The Washington Post .
Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., has separately sought records involving tariff exclusions, including communications involving Apple's former CEO, Tim Cook , as Democrats investigate whether Trump used trade policy to reward political allies and donors.
While donations do not prove wrongdoing or favorable treatment, congressional probes still carry risks: subpoenas consume executive bandwidth, reveal internal communications and generate unpredictable news coverage. Few CEOs relish the idea of sitting at a witness table before lawmakers and television cameras.
"It creates volatility because you get a negative headline," said Monica Guerra , Morgan Stanley's head of policy and geopolitical strategy, who expects Democrats to cast a wide net for their probes.
Democrats have signaled interest in Trump family businesses, government contractors, firms tied to Donald Trump Jr.'s 1789 Capital , and companies associated with Elon Musk and the so-called Department of Government Efficiency .
Then there is the most basic power Congress has: deciding where the money goes.
Trump's 2025 tax cuts and spending law, known as One Big Beautiful Bill , is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion through 2034, according to a KFF analysis of Congressional Budget Office estimates. KFF is a nonpartisan nonprofit that provides health policy information. Meanwhile, new work requirements for Medicaid enrollees are scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, or earlier in some states, while tighter state budgets could mean fewer people are covered and greater pressure on provider payments.
Molina Healthcare generated $32.2 billion , or 75% of its 2025 premium revenue, from Medicaid, according to the company's annual Securities and Exchange Commission filing. In the same filing, Molina warned that losing government contracts or failing to renew them on favorable terms could materially reduce premium revenue.
A Democratic-controlled chamber could not repeal the 2025 law on its own but could use must-pass budget negotiations to seek funding changes or delays to some cuts.
"They're probably going to push back on those Medicaid cuts," Buchbinder told CNBC, noting that preserving coverage could help stabilize enrollment for Medicaid insurers and patient volumes for hospitals.
Hospitals face their own squeeze: fewer insured patients can mean more uncompensated care, while state budget pressure can reduce reimbursement rates, according to KFF. Congress created a $50 billion rural health fund over five years to cushion some of the blow, but KFF and medical providers have said the money would not fully offset the broader Medicaid reductions.
Democratic gains could still cut both ways for healthcare. The same lawmakers seeking to protect Medicaid funding could also intensify scrutiny of insurers, hospitals and drugmakers over prices, coverage and profits.
Defense contractors face a fight over which weapons and programs Congress keeps funding. The White House has requested $1.5 trillion for national defense in fiscal 2027, with a focus on replenishing weapons, bolstering readiness and covering other needs, some tied to the Iran war .
The White House has requested $1.5 trillion for national defense in fiscal 2027, while separately seeking an $87.6 billion supplemental appropriation from Congress for fiscal 2026, driven primarily by military operations related to Iran.
A Democratic Congress could challenge some Iran- and Israel-related spending while pushing for more aid to Ukraine . However, bipartisan consensus on China deterrence, nuclear modernization and missile defense could protect other major programs, according to multiple analysts.
For contractors, the difference could mean billions of dollars in orders.
Lockheed Martin, for example, recently reached a framework agreement with the Pentagon covering 850 F-35 fighter jets over a decade. But the agreement is not yet a finalized contract: Congress must authorize the multiyear purchase and provide the funding.
"You want to be a stock picker and not just ride the whole sector," Guerra told CNBC, pointing to areas such as shipbuilding, autonomous systems and missile defense as likely winners.
For crypto companies, the midterms could determine whether Trump's regulatory shift becomes durable law or remains vulnerable to the next administration. The industry's push for permanence stalled in September, when the Senate failed to advance the Trump-backed Clarity Act , a sweeping market structure bill.
Shares of Coinbase and stablecoin issuer Circle fell as much as 11% when the measure failed.
Getting a bill through the next Congress could come at a price. Democratic gains would give the party more leverage to demand stricter consumer safeguards, limits on yield-bearing stablecoins and tighter scrutiny of Trump's crypto businesses.
"In some ways, the industry doesn't really care who got elected," said Sam Stovall , chief investment strategist at CFRA Research. "They just want to know what the rules are going to be for the coming year."
Banks are looking for durability, too.
Federal regulators estimate their proposed capital overhau l would cut requirements for the largest banks by roughly 4.8% , potentially freeing billions for lending and shareholder payouts. The Federal Reserve writes the rules, but Senate control shapes who fills future vacancies, and congressional committees can pressure regulators through hearings and investigations.
"It's at the regulatory level where stuff can happen that matters," Buchbinder said.

articles.title_orig: You can't escape AI, but you can learn to live with it. Wharton Professor Ethan Mollick explains how.
articles.title_zh: You can't escape AI, but you can learn to live with it. Wharton Professor Ethan Mollick explains how.
articles.content_orig:
Chief Correspondent covering media and technology
You can't make AI go away. How can you live with it?
Or more precisely: How can you make a living in an AI world?
Here are a couple standard answers: "Learn to use AI." Or figure out an AI-proof career, one that can't be automated away. Maybe something with your hands .
Ethan Mollick doesn't think that will work.
Mollick is a Wharton management professor who has become one of the more influential guides to what AI can already do — and what it will mean for people who have to work alongside it. His new book, " Co-Existence ," argues that the models are improving much faster than most people understand, and the only way to deal with their rapid acceleration is to learn how to live with them.
That means acknowledging that a lot of what you can do today will be less useful in the future, and concentrating on the attributes you already have that AI can't replicate.
I talked to Mollick about what AI means for your job, your kids' future, and what happens when the systems that train workers start to break down on my Channels podcast. The following is an edited excerpt of our conversation.
Peter Kafka: People worried about their jobs, or their kids' jobs, are being told to become AI experts — or to find lines of work that are AI-proof, like plumbing or nursing. Is that useful?
Ethan Mollick: I don't think it's very useful. First of all, that's great until PlumBot 6000 comes along. I'm not a robotics expert, but the robotics experts I know went from, "LLMs will never … this AI boom is completely unrelated … robots are hard" to, "Actually there's a thing here."
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
I don't know what the future holds. I don't think anyone does, which is either comforting or very upsetting to hear from somebody who's an AI expert.
Look at the most changed field, which is coding. We already know coding is changing. [But] we aren't even clear whether there are going to be more or less jobs in coding. We know what you do as a coder is going to change and keep changing.
Writing error-free code is now less important than conceiving of what you want to have built. A lot of coders are happier than they've ever been before. Some are sadder. These are evolving jobs.
In the book, I talk about four things that give you at least some advantage. Deep knowledge : knowing an area really well, because that expertise lets you outcompete the AI. Wide knowledge : knowing about lots of different things.
One thing I see in companies is they say, "Our coders are doing design work, our designers are doing coder work, and the marketers are doing business plans." The more you know about a lot of little things, the more AI can help you.
Then there's taste . AI produces a lot. What prevents it from being slop? Your taste about which things to pick.
And finally, agency . I don't think "learning to use AI" means very much right now. We've been testing all the methods we use to teach people how to use AI. None of those tricks work anymore.
Prompting has started to look a lot more like managing. You don't have to do magic words anymore to make the AI do something. Instead, you specify: Here's the product I want, here's how I know it's good, here's how you should test it, here's what you show me partway. Give me five different mockups that I can pick among.
That seems like good news for someone mid-career, who has experience, taste, and has gotten good at their job. But if you're starting out, how do you develop that stuff in a world where AI says, "I'll do the research. I'll write it for you."
There are two problems. One is people as individuals, and the other is the institutions we have for teaching people.
As individuals, we love to cognitively offload stuff. That's what we're built to do. Technology has always been about replacing annoying labor. No one pines for washing dishes by hand once they have a dishwasher.
No one wants to churn their own butter.
My kids don't learn cursive. I don't know how to use a slide rule.
But we're bad at picking which things we want to offload. That's a problem with everyone cheating on homework.
And then there are the institutions. There are two sets of learning institutions for learning how to do a job. One is college and high school education. They're screwed up right now, but we'll figure that out. AI is actually a really good tutor, and we know how to test people without AI: You put them in a classroom with a blue book or have a conversation. We'll have better education as a result, with AI tutoring outside of class and active learning inside of class.
What I'm worried about is the other method, which is apprenticeship.
I send people to a bank, consulting company, audit firm, or car dealership, and they learn the same way everyone always has.
They do grunt work, poorly paid. They might get abused a little bit. The trade is that they learn skills and contacts, and they learn how to do stuff because we force them to do it.
And middle managers get somebody to do their crap work. Even if you're a bad mentor, people still learn the ropes. If they show they can do a good job, they advance. You get the next generation of good employees. It has worked out wonderfully for a few thousand years.
That all broke because the incentives are no longer aligned. As a junior employee, your best bet is to use AI for everything because it's better than you. Junior people are much worse at using AI because they dump everything into Claude and give you Claude's results. How could they tell you whether it's a good report or bad? They haven't built taste.
And managers realize: "Why would I go to an intern when the AI will solve the problem for me, at a better rate?" And company leaders say: "Why would I want to slow this train down? Why would I want worse work from interns?"
The training mechanism was this virtuous cycle, and it is completely shattered.
Either we will have to make more formal education happen — a lot of light, white-collar work will have to look more like welding or plumbing, with a trade-school aspect—or companies are going to have to get serious about mentorship as a real thing they do. It takes time and costs productivity, but you gain the benefit of having junior people.
My fear is that companies will say, "We'll just hire senior people." That's the dangerous area. The talent pipeline ends. There are no replacements.

By SAM MERRIMAN, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT
Published: 20:12 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 22:07 EDT, 1 November 2026
Ministers have been accused of jeopardising national security by prioritising 'diplomatic politeness' with China .
A report from MPs today criticises Labour's approach to Beijing as the 'worst of both worlds'.
In a devastating indictment of its dealings with the communist state, the chairman of the business, innovation, science and trade committee (Bist) said the 'Government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along'.
Firms have missed out on lucrative commercial deals as Britain has been left increasingly exposed to 'unquantified, unmanaged risk', the report adds.
Last night the committee put pressure on the Prime Minister to clarify his stance on closer dealings with the Chinese Communist Party.
'We await confirmation of how much continuity there is between the approaches to China of the Starmer and Burnham governments,' the MPs said.
Last year Labour, under Sir Keir Starmer, refused to publish a Government review of relations with China, releasing only a short summary and arguing that publishing the full findings could damage British interests.
In June, two men were convicted of running 'shadow policing' operations on British soil, spying on Chinese dissidents and MPs who supported them.
Labour ministers have been accused of jeopardising national security by prioritising 'diplomatic politeness' with China. Pictured: PM Andy Burnham, then Mayor of Manchester, with China's Consul General Tang Rui on April 17, 2026
Labour's Ed Miliband shakes hands with Wang Hongzhi, head of China's National Energy Administration, at the China-UK Energy Dialogue in Beijing, China on March 17, 2025
Labour was accused of pandering to China after plans for a new mega embassy on the old Royal Mint site were approved in January, despite spying fears. Pictured: A concept grapohic for the proposed embassy
Labour was accused of pandering to China after plans for a new mega embassy on the old Royal Mint site near the Tower of London were approved in January, despite spying fears.
Shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat has described the report as 'damning' and accused Labour of overseeing a dereliction of its duty to the public.
He told the Daily Mail: 'Labour are distracted and allowing Beijing to dictate terms, risking economic dependence on a hostile China. This is unacceptable. The Government's disjointed, last-minute approach leaves Britain weak and susceptible to Chinese control.'
The report warns that 'low-cost, increasingly sophisticated Chinese-connected technology has proliferated in the UK' and says the Government should create a register of high-risk firms to combat the threat associated with this.
It concludes: 'We are disappointed that, in failing to create a register of high-risk jurisdictions, the Government has prioritised diplomatic politeness over the UK's national security.' However, the Government last night rejected the Bist committee report and said it 'disagrees with its conclusion'.
The committee found that Labour has re-engaged with Beijing 'without establishing the rules of the game'.
Its chairman, Labour MP Liam Byrne, said: 'Businesses cannot plan for the future when the Government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along. Ministers promised clarity and consistency.
'Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the eleventh hour. Britain must shape its own relationship with China, or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.'
China's President Xi Jinping, right, and Britain's then Prime Minister Keir Starmer, left, shake hands before their meeting at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on January 29, 2026
Bill Yuen, 65, (l) and Peter Wai, 41, (r) were convicted in June following a trial at the Old Bailey. Wai was found guilty of running a Chinese 'state intelligence service' on British soil while working as a UK Border Force officer, on the orders of former Hong Kong superintendent Yuen
The report also found products made with slave labour by repressed Uyghur Muslims ending up on British shelves. Pictured: Buildings north of Kashgar in China's northwestern Xinjiang region believed to be a re-education camp where mostly Muslim ethnic minorities are detained
Should Britain risk national security for economic ties and diplomatic relations with China?
Mr Byrne added that 'we should welcome trade that builds Britain's strength' but cease dealings that 'put that strength at risk'.
The committee recognised that disengaging from China is neither realistic nor desirable as annual trade with Beijing is now £140billion a year – about 7 per cent of total UK trade.
However it added that changes need to be made as the Government's decision-making on China – such as the takeover of British Steel from the firm's Chinese owners at a cost of £1.3million a day – has been characterised by 'reactivity, inconsistency, and opacity'.
MPs also raised concerns about the increasing adoption of cheap Chinese electric cars. These devices pose a risk to national security through spying and the ability to control vehicles remotely is a 'potential risk to life', the report adds.
The report is also damning on the risk of products made with slave labour by repressed Uyghur Muslims in the Xinjiang region ending up on British shelves.
In order to reset Britain's relationship with China, MPs have called on the Government to 'insist on fair trade' to create a 'level playing field'. Ministers should also 'prevent the transfer of sensitive technologies and data to China'.
A Government spokesman said: 'Our approach to China is consistent – we will co-operate where we can and challenge where we must.
'Our Trade Strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on national security. Increased discussions with China allow us to directly raise concerns where they arise.'

The spokesman for Iran parliament’s national security committee warned on Monday that a renewed war could spread geographically and strike areas not previously considered targets.
Hassan Ghashghavi said there were places “perhaps no one has thought about so far,” but said he would not discuss details.
He said Iran’s offensive and defensive capabilities had improved since the 12-day war and that a new conflict would bring “more surprises.”
Ghashghavi said an order by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei for an immediate and effective response to threats, without geographical limits, had been issued for implementation and should not remain at the level of analysis and commentary.
The gold, jewelry, silver and coin dealers’ union in Iran’s northeastern city of Mashhad has banned the sale and display of gold products featuring designs associated with the Pahlavi era or the Lion and Sun, according to an official notice to businesses in the sector.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Monday that parties to the Middle East conflict should pursue political solutions rather than resume fighting, during a meeting in Beijing with Iranian national security official Ali Bagheri Kani, China’s Xinhua news agency reported.
Wang also said China supports Iran in safeguarding its sovereignty and security.
Iranian negotiators left Doha on Sunday, but not because of difficulties in talks aimed at ending the US-Israeli war on Iran, Reuters reported on Monday, citing an official briefed on the discussions.
A draft proposal was being circulated for feedback, and a follow-up meeting was possible, the official added.
Iran should extend its missile range beyond 2,000 kilometers and reconsider its nuclear doctrine, including developing the capability to build nuclear weapons, a lawmaker said on Monday.
Mohammad Motamedizadeh said Israel was “at the tip of our blade” and that Iran should also target “the heart of America.” He said Iran could target adversaries’ interests in the United States and Europe if threatened.
He added that there was no reason for Iran to remain in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
He also described Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s remarks about responding to threats “at any level” as a sign of a shift in Iran’s nuclear posture.

Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said Monday that the next move in the standoff with the United States is for President Trump to make.
"The ball is in the U.S. court, because our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran's demands are reasonable and logical," Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists in Tehran.
Baqaei said ongoing negotiations, which have been brokered by Qatar, Pakistan and other mediators, were centered around the a seven-day proposal that Iran originally presented to the U.S. side in September, which calls for frozen Iranian assets to be released, the U.S. naval blockade to be lifted and an end to fighting on all fronts, in exchange for the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and further negotiations on other topics.
President Trump rejected the initial proposal, but both sides have since exchanged revisions, and Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he just needs to make a decision on whether to launch new attacks on Iran, or to make a deal to end the war.
Speaking Sunday to a radio network ahead of a campaign rally in Iowa, Mr. Trump said he would finish with the war soon, "one way or the other."
"Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he said, without offering any further context.
President Trump told reporters Sunday that he'd spoken with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday and had a "very good talk with him."
Mr. Trump gave no details but said the two had discussed the war in Iran.
According to sources cited by Axios , Netanyahu pushed for Mr. Trump to strike Iran but the president wants to let the negotiations play out.
The U.S. and Iran both engaged in indirect talks via mediators led by Qatar who are pushing to strike a deal between both sides before the conflict escalated.
Mr. Trump has repeatedly hinted he is considering resuming attacks on Iran after the midterm elections.
Qatari mediators are leading indirect talks aimed at reaching a deal between the U.S. and Iran, but the closed door negotiations have been punctuated by exchanges of threats between the leaders of both countries.
Iranian negotiators are in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz soon, according to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who added the outcome depends on answers provided by the United States.
On Saturday, President Trump said the U.S. still had to "take care of" one or two more potential targets in Iran, citing a suspected nuclear complex at Pickaxe Mountain. On Sunday he reiterated the threat, saying he may have to give Tehran "the hammer" at some unspecified time.
Meanwhile, Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei warned on Saturday there would be no "geographical limitations" should the fighting with the U.S. resume, adding that there is a "vast theatre" to inflict damage.
Both sides have previously acknowledged that indirect talks are underway but consistently exchange threats.
The United Arab Emirates' presidential adviser said Sunday that his country hopes a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations is possible, but that they are also preparing for the possibility of escalation.
Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Anwar Gargash said Iran's attacks on Gulf countries such as the UAE made this a "watershed year" for the region.
"We don't really want to see another round of confrontation in the region," Gargash told the audience. But he added that his country and the region are braced for the "the worst," referring to the resumption of active hostilities.
The UAE was consistently targeted by Tehran in the opening weeks of the war in retribution for U.S. strikes on Iran, disrupting tourism and daily life, and effectively throwing the security landscape of the region into question.
A vessel was struck on Sunday by "an unknown projectile" in the Strait of Hormuz, a British maritime security agency said, after Qatari media reported an earlier attack on a gas tanker.
Britain's UKMTO maritime agency said "the master of a merchant vessel has relayed a mayday call... stating that another vessel has been struck by an unknown projectile" in the strait.
Earlier, Qatar's state news agency said a Qatari gas tanker had been attacked on Friday with "unidentified objects" while transiting Gulf waters. None of the crew members onboard the vessel were injured, and there was no environmental impact from the attack, the report said.
The attack struck a liquefied natural gas carrier, Al Mayeda, which belongs to the Qatar Gas Transport Company, Qatar News Agency said.
Since the Middle East war began in February, Iran has been targeting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf in an effort to assert control over shipping.
President Trump said he believes the U.S. will soon put the war with Iran away, "one way or the other."
The president was speaking to Right Side Broadcasting Network before a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday.
"We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other," Mr. Trump said. "Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it… The job we've done is amazing."
Earlier Sunday, Iran's top diplomat said he hopes there is "rationality" on the U.S. side as diplomatic efforts seek to avert a return to all-out war.

The Raspberry Pi 5 with 16GB of RAM now costs $385 after an $80 price hike , the latest in a string of increases driven by the ongoing RAM shortage . This configuration launched at $120 and now costs more than triple that price. The 16GB versions of the Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 also got a $40 price hike and now cost between $375 and $415.
According to Raspberry Pi CEO Eben Upton, these price hikes were driven specifically by a lack of “alternative supply” for 16GB DRAM, on top of shortages for other components. Upton says, “Though these increases are unavoidable, we know they are unwelcome news for our customers. We encourage you to make sure you’re not paying for more memory than you need.” Upton suggested using Pis with less memory or older Pi models as alternatives to the pricey 16GB model. Unfortunately, other Raspberry Pi 5 configurations have also gotten more expensive — the 2GB version got a price hike last month.
At $385, the 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 is nearing the price of a desktop mini PC. Upton reiterated the company’s plans to reverse the price hikes, saying, “the current memory landscape is difficult but ultimately temporary, and we look forward to rolling back our price increases when memory costs fall once again.”

articles.title_zh: Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain, some carrying eggs and watermelons
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China's most famous peaks Monday, many carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organizers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.
For hundreds of years, Mount Tai -- the tallest peak in China's eastern Shandong province -- was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors, and it features prominently in Chinese mythology.
But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.
The UNESCO World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed.
Over a 2.4-mile course with more than 1,970 feet of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods such as fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.
A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology -- a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree -- completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.
Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.
The fastest humanoid robot -- belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue -- completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.
Organizers called Mount Tai's rocky terrain a "natural extreme testing ground" that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.
The race, organized by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.

According to Shelley, some smaller Iranian tankers turn off their tracking systems, sail under false flags, or conduct ship-to-ship transfers at sea to evade detection.
The UANI analyst noted that while the U.S. blockade has severely curtailed Iran’s crude oil exports, certain smaller tankers still manage to slip through.
Fox News further reported that China now serves as the destination for almost “all of Iran’s oil and LPG exports,” with Malaysian maritime corridors playing a critical role in sustaining this trade.

Inference refers to the process of running trained AI models to respond to user requests, which involves processing units of data known as tokens. As AI adoption accelerates, the volume of token calls, which refers to AI usage through public cloud service providers, provides an indication of growing demand for AI services.

Ukraine and Russia say their emergency warning apps have been hit by cyber-attacks, causing false alerts to be issued
Moscow says a "massive cyber-attack" has affected its app but insists its wider alert system is "operating as normal" . A Ukrainian espionage group claims the messages included fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia
This comes shortly after Ukraine's air raid warning app sent out false warnings of a radiation threat in Kyiv , following an apparent hack
Ukraine has blamed Russia for the hack on its app, while Moscow is yet to say who it believes is behind the cyber-attack on its system
The alerts in Ukraine were sent out just minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in the front-line Kherson region, our Ukraine reporter Abdujalil Abdurasulov writes
Edited by Toby Mann and Yvette Tan
While we wait for further information on the apparent cyber attacks in Russia and Ukraine, here's the latest on the strikes that were reported overnight.
In a statement on Telegram, Russia's Ministry of Defence says it struck a Ukrainian military cargo vessel at sea 58km south of Odesa overnight.
It says the vessel was "delivering cargo intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces".
Another strike hit a storage site for Ukrainian missile launch systems in the Odesa village of Tuzly, it says.
Meanwhile, a Telegram channel for the city of Odesa says four people were injured in strikes in Odesa overnight. "All received prompt medical assistance," the update says.
It adds that two private homes, a garage and city infrastructure also sustained "significant damage".
The false alerts started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT) on Sunday, with red-level air raids apparently issued nationwide, in Ukrainian.
Additional warnings were issued in Kyiv, with the first reading: "Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48 , which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying". Oreshnik is the name of a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile capable of carrying nuclear or conventional warheads.
A third alert, at 22:49 , again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49 , a fourth alert stated there was a "street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyiv alerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
We don't know much about the alerts sent out in Russia. But as we reported earlier, a Ukrainian espionage group claimed fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia had been sent to users.
Dan Johnson Ukraine correspondent, reporting from Kyiv
Ukraineâs air raid alert app usually warns of incoming Russian drones or missiles.
Last night it issued alerts of a radiological threat, a chemical attack and street fighting here in Kyiv.
The warnings were followed by all clear messages just over an hour later.
The air force issued a statement saying the app had been hacked and reassured citizens there was no imminent threat of nuclear war, blaming Russian interference.
Hours later, Russiaâs emergencies ministry claimed it had also suffered a cyber attack and said people were receiving emails containing fake information.
Itâs not clear if the two incidents are connected.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee, has told the BBC the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko says Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, are used to "practically non-stop alerts".
"Secondly, this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions," he says.
"It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities," adds Merezhko, a member of President Volodymyr Zelensky's Servant of the People party,
Russia and Ukraine both say their emergency alert systems have been hit by cyber-attacks. Here's what we know so far:
The BBC's Newsday programme has just spoken to Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, who describes the hacking of Ukraine's air strike alert system as "concerning".
âI think itâs the first time itâs happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it wonât be the last,â says Lin, who previously served on former US President Barack Obamaâs Commission on Enhancing National Cybersecurity.
âWe donât know how they did it yetâ¦ Maybe in the future theyâll be able to do it more but we just donât know yet.â
Russia and Ukraine have also exchanged strikes targeting each other's energy infrastructure.
Russia said drone strikes hit an "industrial enterprise" east of Moscow overnight, which Ukrainian media identified as the Kstovo oil refinery.
The governor of Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region - home to the Kstovo plant - described a "massive" drone attack during the night and morning.
Gleb Nikitin said significant damage was sustained and warned of power outages and reduced hot water supplies. He said one woman was injured as a result of falling drone debris.
Ukrainian forces have repeatedly attacked Russian oil and gas sites in retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. A Reuters report quoted him as saying the intensity of these strikes were "very high".
Some connections were restored on Sunday.
Aftermath of a Russian drone strike in Kramatorsk, Ukraine on 1 November
The fake alert sent to Russia's emergency app had warned users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".
The alert, which opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of getting lively" also told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".
Emergency alert apps in Ukraine and Russia have been hacked, according to reports.
The Ukraine government's Center for Strategic Communications has blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account, saying one of the alerts was a "message in Russian about Oreshnik".
A few hours later, Moscow also said that its emergency alert app had been hit by a "massive cyber-attack" - but did not immediately say who might be behind it.
Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications has blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account.
It posted a picture showing some of the alerts that had showed up on Ukraine's air raid warning app and asked residents to "disregard" any "strange messages" they might see in the app.
The Russian emergencies ministry says its public alert system is "operating as normal", stressing that citizens are informed of alerts through multiple channels including sirens and loudspeakers, text messages, and TV and radio broadcasts, and that the app is "only an additional, ancillary news service".
"The hacking of the mobile app has not had, and cannot have, any impact on the operation of the public alert system," it said on its Telegram channel.
It said specialists were working to restore normal operation of the mobile app but the situation was "under control".

The rare six-day ceasefire had allowed hundreds to evacuate from Oleshky, in a deal that was brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV.
It was the longest a ceasefire has held since the start of Russiaâs full-scale invasion.

(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices were sharply lower in late U.S. trading Friday, as a technology-led equity market selloff intensified liquidation pressure across precious metals, offsetting the support normally provided by falling Treasury yields and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Crude oil prices climbed more than 2% following another tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz, adding to inflation concerns and expectations that Federal Reserve monetary policy will remain restrictive. Spot gold was trading near $3,879.90 an ounce, down $141.60, or 3.52%, while spot silver was trading near $49.015, down $3.150, or 6.06%, on the session.
Friday's U.S. economic reports presented a mixed picture of moderating wage growth and weakening regional manufacturing activity. The employment cost index increased 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9% in the second quarter. The October Chicago purchasing managers' index declined to 55.3 from 58.8 in September, missing expectations near 56.1 but remaining above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction. Friday's softer wage and manufacturing readings followed Thursday's stronger-than-expected third-quarter gross domestic product report, which showed the U.S. economy expanding at a 3.4% annualized pace , compared with 2.2% in the second quarter. September headline personal consumption expenditures inflation accelerated to 3.6% annually, while core PCE inflation increased to 3.1%, reinforcing concerns about persistent underlying price pressure.
Market positioning remains divided between resilient economic growth, persistent inflation and the growing risk of financial-market instability. The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% Wednesday , with two policymakers favoring an immediate 25-basis-point increase. Interest rate futures continued to reflect substantial expectations for further tightening in December, although Friday's moderating employment costs and sharp equity-market decline provided counterweights to the inflationary implications of strong GDP growth and higher energy prices. Treasury yields fell as investors sought the relative safety of government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year yield retreating toward 4.93% and the two-year yield approaching 4.58%. However, gold continued to decline, suggesting that forced liquidation, portfolio rebalancing and the broader outlook for restrictive monetary policy outweighed immediate safe-haven demand.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a major source of energy-market uncertainty Friday after another commercial tanker was attacked in the strategic waterway. The vessel was struck by explosive devices attached to its hull by a small boat, highlighting the continuing vulnerability of commercial shipping despite regional diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions. Responsibility for the attack had not been established. The incident intensified concerns that renewed military confrontation involving Iran and the United States could further disrupt Middle Eastern energy exports, particularly as markets assessed the possibility of additional military action following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections. Negotiations involving Washington, Tehran and regional mediators have yet to produce a confirmed settlement, leaving disagreements over sanctions, maritime security and the future of commercial access through Hormuz unresolved.
Crude oil futures rose more than 2% Friday, reaching their highest settlements since late April as traders assessed the possibility of renewed disruptions to Gulf energy supplies. December Brent crude futures gained $2.76, or 2.4%, to settle at $117.64 a barrel after reaching $118.00 intraday. articles.title_orig: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
articles.title_zh: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.
The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech that will touch on the issue.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier wrote in the Guardian that he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.
It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and that the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.
Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
In an address to the nation to mark Antigua and Barbuda's independence day, Prime Minister Gaston Browne said the history of slavery was painful and "its consequences have not disappeared with the passage of time".
He said the country's pursuit of reparatory justice deserved "seriousness, sensitivity and sustained international engagement".
Browne went on to say that his government was having these conversations in bilateral discussions with the UK and other Commonwealth countries at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving current problems.
She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."
The King will make his speech at the CHOGM.
He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said.
"You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."
When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to the government's position.
The Caribbean tour has again thrust the King into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion , where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.
Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.
Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology were a matter for government, not the Palace.
"His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to bat for Britain, the Realms and wider Commonwealth."
In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation", and said Britain "must face up to the past".
His separate pledge in his article to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by the King, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.
The King will be giving the opening speech at CHOGM, which gathers leaders from those 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth.
The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua and, as the couple attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island, there was a reminder of what the intended focus of the week will be.
Bishop of North Eastern Caribbean and Aruba, Ernest Flemming, told the congregation the "prosperity" of the Commonwealth must be a "shared prosperity".
"True partnership requires mutual respect, it requires listening, it requires fairness."
A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: "Institutions are under strain across the globe. The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."
The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".
Later on Sunday, the King was left drenched and without an umbrella when a torrential downpour interrupted an Independence Day ceremony.
The Queen was swiftly given an umbrella when the rain started, while the King was seen gesturing to be given one of his own.
It has been a difficult few months for the King, with developments surrounding his brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor , and the publication of a book by his former brother-in-law, Earl Spencer.
In addition, his son, the Duke of Sussex, made a surprise move back to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children in August.
Asked whether the King was confident that his approach to family matters had been the right one in terms of public attitudes towards the institution, the response was concise. "Yes," a senior aide told the BBC. "That is why he takes the actions he does - and has done."
On the serious allegations that have emerged about Meghan's father , Thomas Markle, the Palace did not want to get involved publicly: "We wouldn't comment on private family matters."
The King is also still being treated for cancer. He was diagnosed in early 2024 and the Palace says he remains on a "positive trajectory".
In hot and humid conditions, he will soon celebrate his 78th birthday and will have carried out about 36 engagements by the end of this nine-day tour of the Caribbean.

articles.title_zh: Binance sees $3.64 billion in net outflows as withdrawals resume after massive hack
articles.content_orig:
Binance said it recorded $3.64 billion in net outflows after reopening withdrawals on Sunday following a $6.3 billion hack, as customers rushed to move funds off the platform.
The exchange processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits between 6 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. UTC on Nov. 1, Binance said in a post on X.
The resulting net outflows represented 2.1% of Binance's $171 billion in total assets, based on its latest available proof-of-reserves data as of Oct. 28.
Binance said withdrawal volumes had declined and were stabilizing following an initial spike, while deposit volumes remained substantial.
The exchange began restoring withdrawals in phases at 6 a.m. UTC on Sunday, with services resuming across all 15 networks and assets included in the initial phase by 12:36 p.m. UTC. It said testing was continuing for the remaining networks and assets.
Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao sought to reassure users following the breach, writing on X that "98% choose to stay!" He said most of the net outflows occurred within the first couple of hours after withdrawals resumed. "Trust isn't earned by what you say in good times. It's earned by what you do in hard times," Zhao added.
The withdrawals followed a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance last week. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korean hackers, identifying the operation as TraderTraitor.
The exchange has said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than pass the losses on to users.
Binance said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount, up from 90% in its previous update. The exchange said the remaining 5% consisted of less liquid tokens that would take longer to source in the quantities required.

Iran likely struck a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz on November 1 as part of its efforts to disrupt civilian shipping. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization (UKMTO) reported on November 1 that an unidentified projectile struck a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.[1] The Iranian regime calculates that it can pressure the United States into a diplomatic settlement that favors Iran by disrupting shipping and keeping oil prices high. Iran continues to be the only threat to civilian shipping in the strait.

The Houthis are continuing to attempt to advance southeastward from Taiz Governorate into Lahij Governorate, potentially to set conditions to besiege or capture Aden City. A Marib-based Yemeni journalist reported that Houthi fighters advanced onto elevated terrain in al Maqatirah District, Lahij Governorate, on November 1.[2] Pro-Yemeni government media reported that Yemeni government reinforcements deployed to the district later on November 1.[3] The source did not specify whether Yemeni government-aligned forces recaptured territory in al Maqatirah District, which suggests that the area remains contested at the time of this writing.[4] Yemeni government-aligned forces reportedly repelled another Houthi attempt to advance southeastward from southern Taiz Governorate into al Maqatirah District on October 30. The Houthis likely seek to capture terrain that overlooks Tur al Balah District and leads to Aden City. Such territory would support a potential Houthi effort to besiege or capture Aden City.[5]
Yemeni government-aligned forces continued to engage Houthi fighters in central Jawf Governorate on November 1. A Marib-based Yemeni journalist reported that Yemeni government-aligned forces repelled a Houthi attempt to advance to Jabal Huwayshiyan from the northeast. Jabal Huwayshiyan is a mountain range overlooking al Hazm, the governorate’s capital.[6] Yemeni government-aligned forces recaptured Jabal Huwayshiyan between October 30 and 31.[7] Yemeni government-aligned forces are likely attempting to recapture territory in central Jawf Governorate as part of an effort to set conditions to recapture al Hazm.[8]
Saudi Joint Forces Command spokesperson Major General Turki al Maliki announced that Saudi Arabia targeted unspecified “vital resources” in Houthi-controlled Dhamar and Hudaydah governorates on November 1.[9] Pro-Yemeni government media and Houthi media reported that Saudi Arabia struck Houthi troop concentrations in Dhamar Governorate.[10] Houthi media separately reported that Saudi Arabia struck oil infrastructure in Bajil District, Hudaydah Governorate.[11] Saudi Arabia previously struck Houthi oil and fuel storage infrastructure in Yemen on October 13, likely to both maximize economic pressure on the Houthi political organization and constrain the Houthis’ ability to sustain their military forces.[12]
Saudi air defenses intercepted one Houthi ballistic missile and one drone launched toward Saudi Arabia’s southern region on November 1. [13] The Houthis have not claimed the attack as of this writing. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi critical infrastructure as part of the Houthis’ ongoing strike campaign to compel Saudi Arabia to halt military operations against the Houthis and accept the Houthis’ demands, which include lifting Saudi controls on Houthi-controlled ports and airports and granting the Houthis control over Yemen’s oil and gas resources.[14]

articles.title_orig: Huawei in the Dock
articles.title_zh: Huawei in the Dock
articles.content_orig:
Good evening. If all had gone according to plan, the United States v Wanzhou Meng and Huawei Technologies would have opened in a federal courtroom in the waning months of President Donald Trump’s first term. And what a trial it would have been: an heir to one of China’s most successful and strategically important companies, detained in Canada and extradited to the U.S., on trial for allegedly lying to banks about Huawei operations in Iran that were in violation of American sanctions on the country. But Xi Jinping forestalled that humiliating spectacle by ordering the arrest of two Canadians in China, Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, and not releasing them until the U.S. and Canada allowed Meng, the daughter of Huawei’s founder, to return to China in September 2021. Five years later the United States v Huawei Technologies , minus Meng, is finally underway. Noah Berman reports from the courtroom in Brooklyn.
In other articles, Leon Panetta speaks with Bob Davis about his dealings with China as a Congressman, White House Chief-of-Staff, CIA Director and Secretary of Defense.
Noah Berman on DayOne , the Singaporean data center operator that is helping Chinese companies realise their AI ambitions.
In The Big Picture , Savannah Billman writes about the enormous popularity of AI-generated “short dramas” in China.
Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin on the barriers to a common-sense Sino-U.S. AI safety agreement .
And finally, be sure to catch up on the latest episode of our weekly podcast , with Peiyue Wu talking about her recent cover on dual-use farms in China.
Want this emailed directly to your inbox? Sign up to receive our free newsletter.
In 2021 Meng Wanzhou, daughter of Huawei Technologies founder Ren Zhengfei, signed a “statement of facts” to resolve U.S. charges against her. According to that statement, “Ms. Meng [told HSBC] … Huawei’s relationship with Skycom was ‘normal business cooperation’ and … she described Skycom as a … ‘third party Huawei works with’ in Iran … Those statements were untrue because, as Ms. Meng knew, … Huawei controlled Skycom.” The U.S. let Meng go regardless because the Chinese government made it clear that it would not release two Canadian hostages until she was freed. Five years later the U.S. government’s case against Huawei is finally underway in New York, with Meng safely back in China.
Leon Panetta fought with, and engaged with China over a long career in politics. The former Congressman, White House Chief of Staff, CIA Director and Defense Secretary talks with Bob Davis about why China thinks President Trump is good for China.
“If China senses weakness, they’ll take advantage of it,” Panetta says. “Right now, China is in a stronger position because we’re locked in a war in Iran, our economy is being impacted by that war, and there’s a lot of unpredictability about the U.S. China has been able to take advantage in areas where once we had some influence, particularly in the Pacific.”
Illustration by Lauren Crow
The U.S. government doesn’t want America’s best chips to power Chinese data centers that would then help Chinese companies hone their AI models and applications. DayOne, a Singapore-based data center provider, profits from this by building data centers in Southeast Asia where Chinese AI firms can legally access America’s best chips. Noah Berman looks at DayOne and the IPO prospectus it has just issued. “DayOne’s rise,” he writes, “illustrates how companies can profit, and even gain backing from American investors, as U.S. export controls lead Chinese companies to seek access to data centers overseas.”
Are you, like the Old Dad who writes this newsletter, also a parent who dreads the short videos on YouTube and elsewhere that so easily reel in your kids? Alas, writes Savannah Billman , if China is anything to go by — as it increasingly is when it comes to tech trends — the madness is only going to get worse. Almost 900 million (!) Chinese people are watching AI-generated “short dramas”, issued as a seemingly endless stream of two-minute videos, on a new generation of apps tailored to the new genre. Over the first half of this year alone about 267,000 AI short videos were released. Ugh.
Recent steps taken towards the establishment of a U.S.-China AI incident-reporting channel are important, write Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin . But, they add, there is “a more pressing issue: frontier AI companies currently do not provide the information they need”.

articles.title_orig: AI investors hedge against losses amid tech stock selloff
articles.title_zh: AI investors hedge against losses amid tech stock selloff
articles.content_orig:
Investor enthusiasm for artificial intelligence's potential to transform the global economy has fueled massive bets on the sector; however, growing concerns about a possible downturn are prompting investors to seek financial protection against losses, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday.
“We’re seeing really significant demand from folks looking to protect downside,” said Stephen Solaka, a senior vice president at Gateway Investment Advisers.
Investors and technology executives are increasingly turning to financial instruments such as put options and credit-default swaps to protect their investments.
Put options give investors the right to sell shares at a predetermined price before a specified date. For shareholders seeking protection, these contracts can limit potential losses if stock prices fall sharply, although investors must pay a premium for that protection.
A combination of rising borrowing costs for major data center projects and chip purchases, falling share prices among AI companies, and a broader stock market selloff has heightened concerns about the sector's financial outlook.
Friday's technology stock selloff wiped out more than $1 trillion in market value. The Nasdaq 100 index fell 3.4%, while the broader S&P 500 dropped 1.8%. The S&P 500's technology sector was hit particularly hard, declining more than 4.2%, NBC News reported Friday.
The growing demand for financial protection comes as AI companies continue seeking enormous amounts of capital to fund infrastructure development and expansion.
According to Solaka, some investors have accumulated such substantial gains from technology stocks that they now prioritize protecting their wealth over pursuing further returns.
“These people have made so much money, they’re quitting to hedge their stock,” Solaka said, adding that some companies restrict employees’ trades.
For example, trading in put options tied to AI cloud infrastructure company CoreWeave surged to record levels in October and remained elevated, according to data from Cboe Global Markets.
Investors are also turning to credit-default swaps, financial contracts that protect against a borrower failing to repay its debt.
According to the report, the cost of insuring against debt defaults by major technology companies, including Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle, rose over the past month to its highest level since 2021.
“There were no exceptions, suggesting broad market concern about the sector rather than idiosyncratic credit events at individual companies,” said Eugene Grinberg, a co-founder of bond data provider Solve.
As investment in AI infrastructure grows, trading firm Jump Trading has begun offering financial contracts that allow companies to protect themselves against a potential collapse in the price of computing power.
For example, companies renting out Nvidia chips could use these contracts to lock in a minimum rental price, protecting revenue if demand for AI computing power falls.
The growing demand for financial protection is reminiscent of the events depicted in The Big Short , when investors used credit-default swaps to bet against mortgage-backed securities before the 2008 financial crisis. Unlike those investors, however, many of today's technology shareholders are not necessarily betting on a market collapse, but seeking to protect gains accumulated during the AI boom.
